name: Erik Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Erik. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to companies, unions or political parties, and what you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a troubleshooter, which means I'm on my own in a single truck instead of with a crew. When the power goes off somewhere in the southern suburbs, I'm the first one there. I find out what's wrong, fix it if it's a blown fuse or a loose connection, and call in the crew if it's a broken pole or a downed line. Some days it's six call-outs, some days it's one big one that takes all afternoon.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being trusted to work alone. Nobody's watching, it's me and the fault. What wears me out is the standby weeks, sleeping with the phone on the pillow. I married Lucia two years ago, she's a receptionist at a dental practice in town, and we rent a flat above a bakery on Mill Street. We've got about three months saved, and we want to start a family soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can stop hearing about it. At the depot I'd say the trucks still need drivers and the faults still need finding. I'd maybe share a joke about it in the football club group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means nothing for me. The fault-finding app on my tablet might get a bit smarter, which would be handy. Lucia's practice already has a booking bot and it hasn't changed much for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal, really. I'd keep doing standby weeks, because the standby money is what's building our savings. Lucia and I would start trying for a baby next year, like we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, even. It's the life we're already building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the booking bot at Lucia's practice. What does it actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It answers the phone after hours and books check-ups. My wife Lucia says the booking bot at her dental practice gets half the bookings wrong, so she spends Monday morning fixing them. In this picture that's as far as it goes, so her job's safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about money that worries you, even if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, a bit. The flat above the bakery is fine for two, but not for three. We'd need a bigger place within a couple of years, and prices round here don't go down.

say: Good, now we can **stop hearing about it**.
The **trucks still need drivers** and the faults still need finding.
think: It means **nothing** for my job, though the fault-finding app might get smarter.
Lucia's **booking bot** at the dental practice hasn't changed much for her.
do: Keep doing **standby weeks** to build savings.
Start trying for a **baby next year** as planned.
Look for a **bigger place** within a couple of years.
feel: **Calm**, even pleased; it's the life they're already building.
S0.quote: My wife Lucia says the booking bot at her dental practice gets half the bookings wrong, so she spends Monday morning fixing them.
fieldNote: Erik works **alone** and values the trust that comes with it.
His plans are about **family**: a baby next year and a bigger flat.
The only pressure he names is **rent**, which predates any AI question.

steps.text: Keep taking standby weeks to build up the savings
Start trying for a baby with Lucia next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress and you can't stop progress. At the football club I'd tell the younger lads to do an apprenticeship, because hands-on work lasts longer. Online I'd keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's Lucia's job I'd worry about, not mine. Booking and answering customers is exactly what's on that list. If her practice decides the bot is good enough, she's out, and that's a third of our income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Lucia to look at a dental nurse course, because that's hands-on and they're always short. I'd take more standby weeks to cover the gap while she studied. And we'd put the baby off for a year until we know where her job stands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for me, worried for her. It's strange. I always thought my wife Lucia had the safe indoor job, and now her booking work is exactly what's on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put the baby off. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not well, at first. Lucia's mum keeps asking when, and so does mine. But I'd rather tell them we waited a year than tell them we can't pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your own work in this picture? Does anything change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork, mostly. I already ask one of those AI apps to help me write up fault reports sometimes. In this picture the dispatch side gets automated, so a computer would decide which call I go to next, and I'd probably have to trust it.

say: It's **progress**, and you can't stop progress.
I'd tell the younger lads at the **football club** to do an apprenticeship.
think: It's his wife Lucia's **reception job** at risk, not his.
If her practice trusts the bot, they lose **a third** of our income.
do: Push Lucia towards a **dental nurse course**, a hands-on role that's always short.
Take **more standby weeks** to cover the gap while she studies.
Put the **baby off** for a year until her job is clear.
feel: **Uneasy** for himself and **worried** for his wife.
Surprised that her **indoor job** turned out to be the less safe one.
S1.quote: I always thought my wife Lucia had the safe indoor job, and now her booking work is exactly what's on the list.
fieldNote: The household risk sits with Lucia's **reception work**, which is high on thinking AI.
Erik's own job is **safe**, but a third of household income is exposed, so he is anxious.
He'd rather **delay the baby** than face family questions about money later.

steps.text: Help Lucia enrol on a dental nurse course this year
Take extra standby weeks to cover the gap while Lucia studies
Put off trying for a baby by a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three pictures share an end point. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should've been more careful, and that people like me need to hear a plan. At work I'd say what everyone would say, that we've still got a few years. I'd stay off the internet, it would be full of nonsense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Lucia's job goes almost straight away, and mine goes in 2031 when the robots come. A truck with a robot in it could do half my call-outs. I'd be thirty when the robots arrive, with no house, maybe a baby, and no trade left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, we'd cut everything, no holiday and no new car, and try to get to six months of savings. I'd apply for a substation technician job, because the big equipment feels further from robots than my truck. And we'd probably move in with my parents for a year to save the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Not panicking, because there are still three years before my part goes. But Lucia would be out of work, and I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move in with your parents. How would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cramped. They've got a spare room and a dog that hates me. But that's what family is for, and I'd rather lean on my dad than on the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still have three years. What would you use them for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learning the substation side properly, the protection relays and the switching, and getting a qualification on paper. If robots come for the lines, someone still has to keep the big stuff running and be responsible for it. I'd want to be that person.

say: We should have been **more careful**, and workers need to hear a plan.
At work I'd say we've still got **a few years**.
think: His wife Lucia's **job goes first**, and his goes in 2031.
A **truck with a robot** in it could do half my call-outs.
do: Cut holidays and the **new car** to reach six months of savings.
Apply for a **substation technician** job, which feels further from robots.
Move in with his **parents** for a year to save the rent.
feel: **Scared** and lying awake, though not panicking because of the **three-year gap**.
S2.quote: A truck with a robot in it could do half my call-outs.
fieldNote: Erik expects **both incomes** to fall: his wife's soon, his own by 2031.
He'd lean on **family** rather than government, true to his traditional outlook.
He sees **substations** as a safer place to wait out the robots.

steps.text: Drop the holiday and new car to reach six months saved
Apply for a substation technician job within the year
Move into his parents' spare room for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready, if you take it seriously. At the football club I'd tell people not to panic but not to sit still either. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's tight but doable. Lucia has time to finish the dental nurse course before the thinking AI arrives in 2031. I'd have until about 2034, when I'd be thirty-four, to get onto the substation side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company for the substation protection course, which they run every spring. Lucia would start her dental nurse training next year. We'd still have a baby, but in a couple of years, once she's qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not stuck. The fast picture felt like being in the passenger seat, and with five years we'd have our hands on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of this plan for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Waiting, probably. I'm not someone who jumps at things, I like to see other people go first. But with five years, I can watch the first lads who move to substations and then follow them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the company didn't offer the course, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd pay for it myself, about twelve hundred pounds, out of the savings. It would hurt, but it's cheaper than finding out at thirty-four that I've got nothing to sell.

say: Five years is **enough to get ready** if you take it seriously.
I'd tell the **football club** not to panic, but not to sit still.
think: It's **tight but doable** for both of us.
His wife Lucia retrains before **2031**, and he moves to **substations** before 2034.
do: Ask for the **substation protection course** next spring.
Support Lucia starting her **dental nurse training** next year.
Have a **baby later**, in a couple of years, once she's qualified.
feel: **Worried**, but with hands **on the wheel** instead of in the passenger seat.
S3.quote: The fast picture felt like being in the passenger seat, and with five years we'd have our hands on the wheel.
fieldNote: Erik's steady style shows: he'd **watch others move first**, then follow.
He'd pay **£1,200** himself for the course if the company didn't.
Family plans are **delayed**, not cancelled, which matters to him.

steps.text: Sign up for the company's spring substation protection course
Pay £1,200 from savings for the course if work won't
Plan a baby for two years' time, after Lucia qualifies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, so there's no excuse. I'd say it to the younger lads at the club, especially the ones going to university for jobs a computer will do. Learn a trade and learn the next trade after it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd be fine. Ten years is enough for Lucia to retrain, for me to move to substations, and for us to buy a house. By 2039 I'd be thirty-nine with a family, and I'd rather face it then than now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the substation course in the next couple of years without rushing. We'd have the baby next year like we planned, and buy a small house within three years. Lucia would do her dental nurse training part time once the baby's at nursery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little uneasy, because it's the same end point and I'm not sure what substations look like in 2039. But we'd have time to see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather face it at thirty-nine than now. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because at thirty-nine I'd have a house, a skill and a family behind me. Right now I've got a rented flat above a bakery and three months of savings. Ten years turns a scare into a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big Joe, our foreman, who's fifty-five and the best lineworker I know. In ten years he's retiring anyway, so he might be the lucky one. It's the twenty-year-old apprentices I'd worry about, the ones just starting now.

say: Ten years is a **fair warning**, so there's no excuse.
Learn a trade, then **learn the next trade** after it.
think: Ten years is enough to **retrain, move and buy** a house.
At **thirty-nine** with a family, I'd rather face it then than now.
do: Do the **substation course** over the next couple of years.
Have the **baby next year** and buy a small house within three years.
Back his wife Lucia doing **part-time dental nurse** training later.
feel: Mostly **calm**, a little **uneasy** about what substations will look like.
S4.quote: Ten years turns a scare into a plan.
fieldNote: With a decade, Erik **keeps the family timeline** and adds a career move.
He worries most for **young apprentices**, not the older crew near retirement.
His advice is distinctly traditional: **trades over university**.

steps.text: Take the substation protection course within two years
Buy a small house in the southern suburbs within three years
Have a baby with Lucia next year as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Lucia's job goes first and mine follows, and we'd have no house and no time. What would help is the company running the substation courses for line staff now, and apprenticeships for the new jobs, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about couples. Everyone asks about my job, but our house runs on two wages, and it turns out the one in the warm office is the one at risk. Nobody tells you that when you're choosing a career at sixteen.

headlineQuote: Our house runs on two wages, and it turns out the one in the warm office is the one at risk.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old troubleshooter** who works alone from a single truck in the southern suburbs.
He's married to Lucia, a **dental receptionist**, and they rent above a bakery while planning a family.
In the middle pictures he worries more for **his wife's job** than his own.
In fast AGI he expects **both incomes** to fall and would move in with his parents.
With more time he plans a **substation move** and keeps family plans largely intact.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his wife's job goes first and his follows with no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Company **substation courses** for line staff now, and **apprenticeships** for new jobs rather than handouts.
